A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 35 pages of v3.pdf and 30 pages of v4.pdf were readable, including equations, proofs, figures, tables and references. Neither supplied PDF contains a separate appendix.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original experiments on synthetic cubic-regularized bilinear problems and AUC optimization using a9a, covetype and w8a.

after.justification: Section 5 reports original synthetic and AUC optimization experiments, with revised convergence curves in Figures 1 and 2.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 replace separate cubic regularization of the x and y updates with a joint-norm term, 6rho||Delta z||Delta z, in a nonlinear equation. Stepsize intervals also change. Section 4.3 replaces the generalized mirror-prox/semismooth Newton subroutine with scalar Newton iterations using a reusable Schur decomposition.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic task and AUC optimization on a9a, covetype and w8a. The changed dataset sample counts concern experimental settings rather than additional task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: External comparator membership remains EG1, OGDA1, EG2 and OGDA2 in Figure 1, and SEG and SOGDA in Figure 2. However, Algorithm 2, explicitly used as the reference against Algorithm 3 in the AUC comparison, adopts the revised regularization and Newton subroutine.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes reported sample counts from 48,842 to 32,561 for a9a and 64,700 to 49,749 for w8a. AUC experiments change kappa_m from 0.1 to 10^-6 and the sampling coefficient from 5 to 20. Synthetic experiments switch from Algorithm 1 to Algorithm 2 with tau_0=0 and kappa_m=10^-8. These substantially revise the reported evaluation settings.

E4.justification: The retained subsampling comparison in Section 5.2 examines whether Algorithm 3 preserves solution quality while requiring fewer samples than Algorithm 2. Figure 2 revises this evidence under stricter solving accuracy and a larger sampling coefficient. No new robustness, distribution-shift or error-analysis study appears.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. No uncertainty-reporting practice is added or removed.

E6.justification: Both figures replace the reported convergence trajectories and Figure 1 timings. For example, Figure 2's covetype curves terminate around 10^-7 in v4 rather than 10^-5 in v3. Broad second-order and subsampling advantages remain. These are revised results under changed methods and settings, not controlled same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 replaces the mirror-prox/SSN analysis with new scalar-function propositions and Theorem 4.6 on global linear and local quadratic Newton convergence. Theorem 4.13 adds a total arithmetic-complexity claim. Outer convergence proofs, constants and the inexact-method gap radius also change. The new convexity assertion has a substantive mathematical problem described in the overall assessment.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion add a central claim of sharper arithmetic complexity: one Schur decomposition per subproblem and O(log log(1/epsilon)) cheaper linear solves. V3 primarily emphasizes optimal outer iteration complexity and a distinct analysis for unbounded domains; v4 shifts the contribution toward inexact methods and explicit subproblem costs.

C2.justification: V4 removes v3's explicit qualification that the cited lower bound assumes linear-span algorithms. Section 4.3 also replaces discussion of SSN's local convergence neighborhood and solver-choice limitations with discussion of scalar Newton convergence and why analyses requiring symmetric matrices do not directly apply. The principal empirical qualifications remain.

D1.justification: The implementation description replaces cone projections, generalized Jacobians, GMRES and SSN safeguards with Schur-factor reuse and two linear solves per scalar Newton iteration. Experimental tolerances and sampling parameters are revised, and MATLAB changes from R2021b to R2023b. Hardware and the dataset access URL remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 argues that its unbounded-domain analysis substantially differs from Perseus; v4 describes the analysis as similar and simpler, emphasizing different inexactness and complexity contributions. Comparisons with Adil et al. and Jiang and Mokhtari are substantially expanded around solver costs. Conn et al. is added, while numerous SSN-related references are removed. The Perseus publication update itself is not a new work.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution narrative and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Sections 3–4 adopt compact operator notation, shorten the extragradient explanation and extensively revise the algorithm and proof exposition. The overall section sequence remains recognizable.

P2.justification: Algorithm boxes are condensed, Table 1 moves ahead of Section 5.1, and figures change axis ranges and legend arrangements. The same table structure and six-panel/three-panel figure organization remain. Figure 2's caption incorrectly mentioning a time row is unchanged in both PDFs.

improvement.justification: V4 offers a simpler solver description and more explicit cost accounting, but its central new guarantee has a mathematical defect. Substituting the permitted case f(x,y)=xy, zhat=(0,1) and rho=1/6 into Eq. (4.11) gives phi(lambda)=1/sqrt(1+lambda^2)-lambda, which is concave near zero, contradicting Proposition 4.5 used in Theorem 4.6. Thus the claimed complexity improvement lacks the stated justification. Presentation gains coexist with this central proof problem, and changed experimental settings prevent a controlled performance comparison; a reliable net quality judgment is therefore unclear.
